entries.ipa: /əˈtrɪbjətəbəl tu/, weak /əˈtrɪbjətəbəl tə/
entries.register: formal — audits, reports, epidemiology, and the courts
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (attributable to having used last year's figures). Never a finite clause — attributable to the fact that is the clause form, and it is clumsy enough that because is nearly always better.
entries.pattern: [noun] is attributable to [noun phrase] / [noun] attributable to [noun phrase] / directly / largely / wholly / partly / in part attributable to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: This is the phrase the whole due to rule is built on: the traditional test for due to is whether attributable to can be swapped in, and where it can, due to is safe under every analysis. Like adjectival due to, it follows be or postmodifies a noun and does not front: Attributable to fog, the flight was canceled is not English, where Due to fog, ... at least gets argued about. Against because of, it is cooler and more quantitative, and it is the word of choice wherever a share of an effect is being assigned rather than a whole one.
entries.meaning: Assigns an effect, or a measured portion of one, to a cause. The object is the cause and the noun in front of the phrase is the effect, which puts it on the same side of the direction trap as as a result of.
examples: Most of the decline is attributable to a single bad quarter.
Roughly a third of the increase is attributable to population growth alone.
Deaths attributable to secondhand smoke have fallen by half since 1990.
The cost overrun is attributable to delays nobody could have foreseen.
Losses attributable to the outage were covered under the policy.
The discrepancy is attributable to having used last year's figures.
Only a small part of the warming is attributable to natural variation.

entries.ipa: /bɪˈkɔz əv/ or /bɪˈkʌz əv/, weak /bɪˈkəz əv/, casual /ˈkʌzə/
entries.register: neutral — the default causal preposition of American English
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund (because of being late), or a fused relative, which is still a noun phrase (because of who he knows, because of what she said). Never a finite clause and never a that-clause. The clause form is the conjunction because standing alone — because it rained, never because of it rained and never because of that it rained.
entries.pattern: [clause] because of [noun phrase] / Because of [noun phrase], [clause] / because of [verb-ing] / partly / largely / mainly / only / precisely because of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Because + clause against because of + noun phrase is the cleanest preposition/conjunction pair in the language: We stayed home because it rained / We stayed home because of the rain. Against due to, because of is adverbial by nature and no editor has ever objected to it, which makes it the safe choice whenever you are unsure. Against owing to and on account of, it is the plain, unmarked word. The internet construction because science, because reasons puts a bare noun after because alone; it is a deliberate joke and is not standard English.
entries.meaning: Names the cause of whatever the main clause reports. It modifies the verb or the entire clause, and that adverbial job is exactly what the traditional usage rule reserved for it and denied to due to. It is neutral about whether the cause is welcome, which is what separates it from thanks to (grateful or sarcastic), courtesy of (wry), and owing to (formal).
examples: The flight was canceled because of fog.
Because of the strike, deliveries are running two days late.
She missed the deadline because of a family emergency.
He got the job because of who he knows, not what he knows.
Because of being out of the country all spring, he never received the notice.
Attendance is down, mostly because of the parking.
We're only here because of you.

entries.ipa: /baɪ ˈrizən əv/, weak /bə ˈrizən ə/
entries.register: legal and formal — outside statutes and pleadings it sounds stilted
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically an abstract one (by reason of insanity, by reason of age). A gerund is possible (by reason of having served twenty years) but uncommon. Never a finite clause — the clausal form is the archaic by reason that.
entries.pattern: [clause] by reason of [noun phrase] / [noun] by reason of [noun phrase] / not guilty by reason of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Because of means the same thing and is shorter. By reason of survives because legal drafting is conservative and because a handful of fixed phrases have hardened around it — not guilty by reason of insanity, disqualified by reason of age. Do not confuse it with by virtue of, which names a qualification that enables something rather than a cause that produces it: you hold the seat by virtue of your office and you lose it by reason of your conviction.
entries.meaning: The formal, chiefly legal way of naming a cause or a ground. In modern American writing it appears almost entirely in statutes, insurance policies, and court filings, plus the set phrases those documents have pushed out into general use.
examples: He was found not guilty by reason of insanity.
No applicant may be refused by reason of race, religion, or national origin.
The lease terminates by reason of the tenant's default.
Benefits were denied by reason of his failure to file on time.
She was excused from jury service by reason of ill health.
Any loss by reason of fire is covered under Section 4.

entries.ipa: /baɪ ˈvɜrtʃu əv/, weak /bə ˈvɜrtʃu ə/
entries.register: formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (by virtue of being the oldest). Never a finite clause — for a clause you need by virtue of the fact that, which is heavy enough that because is almost always the better answer.
entries.pattern: [clause] by virtue of [noun phrase] / By virtue of [noun phrase], [clause] / by virtue of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: By virtue of names a qualification — a status, office, property, or fact that entitles or enables — where because of names a plain cause. He got in by virtue of his last name says the name functioned as a credential; he got in because of his last name says only that it was the reason. Against by dint of, which names effort rather than standing: by dint of hard work, but by virtue of seniority. Virtue here carries its old sense of power, efficacy, not moral goodness.
entries.meaning: Names the status, office, property, or established fact that entitles or enables the main event — the cause understood as a qualification rather than as a force.
examples: By virtue of her office, the vice president presides over the Senate.
He inherited the title by virtue of being the eldest son.
The clause is enforceable by virtue of Section 12 of the agreement.
By virtue of its size alone, the company sets the price for the whole region.
She had access to the files by virtue of her security clearance.
Sound travels faster through steel by virtue of its density.

entries.ipa: /ˈkɜrtəsi əv/, weak /ˈkɜrtəsiə/
entries.register: neutral, and heavily journalistic — captions, credit lines, sportswriting
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person, organization, or thing. No gerund, and never a finite clause. In photo credits it also appears bare, with the of dropped: photo courtesy the Newberry Library.
entries.pattern: [clause], courtesy of [noun phrase] / Courtesy of [noun phrase], [clause] / (credit line) Photograph courtesy of [name] / by courtesy of [noun phrase] (older, more formal)
entries.contrast: Thanks to with the credit spelled out. Both can be sincere or sarcastic, but courtesy of leans harder on agency — the thing named actually supplied the result — and it is far more common at the end of a sentence, tacked on as an afterthought, than at the front.
entries.meaning: 1. Supplied by; with the permission or generosity of. The literal credit line of captions and acknowledgments. 2. Caused by, with a wry tip of the hat. The news and sports use, where the cause is as often unwelcome as welcome.
examples: Photograph courtesy of the National Archives.
Everyone got a ride home, courtesy of her uncle's van.
The map is reproduced courtesy of the state historical society.
The Rangers won it in overtime, courtesy of a deflection off a defenseman's skate.
Half of downtown was dry by noon, courtesy of a burst main on Sixth Street.
He spent the afternoon in the emergency room, courtesy of a ladder he should have thrown out years ago.
Video courtesy of KTLA; used with permission.
The lights came back on a little after four, courtesy of a crew that had been out since dawn.

entries.ipa: /ˈdu tu/, weak /ˈdu tə/ (British /ˈdjuː/)
entries.register: neutral, with a live usage dispute over sense 2
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (due to being understaffed). Never a finite clause — for a clause you need due to the fact that, which spends nine syllables on what because does in two. Note that be due to + a bare infinitive (the train is due to arrive at six) is a completely different construction: the adjective due plus a real infinitive, meaning scheduled.
entries.pattern: [noun] is due to [noun phrase] / [noun] due to [noun phrase] / [clause] due to [noun phrase] / Due to [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: This is the single most-taught prescriptive rule about causal prepositions and the one most widely ignored. Traditionalists allow due to only where attributable to would fit and where it attaches to a noun, and prescribe because of or owing to everywhere else. Because of is never wrong; due to sometimes is, depending entirely on your reader.
entries.meaning: 1. Attributable to; caused by — adjectival, after be or modifying a noun. The delay was due to fog. 2. Because of — adverbial, modifying the whole clause. Standard in American English, still contested. Due to fog, the flight was canceled.
examples: The delay was due to fog over the bay.
Most of the increase is due to a change in how the data is collected.
Absences due to illness must be reported by nine.
Errors due to rounding may make the columns disagree.
Due to the holiday, there will be no pickup on Monday.
The clinic cut its hours due to being understaffed all summer.
Two flights were canceled due to mechanical problems.
The shortfall was due to a single contract nobody had budgeted for.
Service was suspended due to flooding on the lower platform.

entries.ipa: /fɔr ˈlæk əv/, weak /fɚ ˈlæk ə/, also /fər/, stressed for /fɔr/
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically a bare one with no article — for lack of evidence, for lack of funding, for lack of a better word. A gerund is possible but rare. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] for lack of [noun phrase] / For lack of [noun phrase], [clause] / for lack of a better [noun] / for lack of anything better
entries.contrast: For lack of and for want of are one preposition in two vocabularies — lack is the everyday word, want the literary one — and for lack of is the one to use in ordinary American prose. Both name a missing cause: the reason something failed is that something else was absent. Watch the direction against because of: because of the evidence means the evidence caused it, for lack of evidence means the absence did.
entries.meaning: Names an absence as the cause: the thing failed because something necessary was not there.
examples: The case was dismissed for lack of evidence.
The project died for lack of funding.
He agreed, for lack of a better option.
Call it a hunch, for lack of a better word.
Three houses burned for lack of a working hydrant.
She stayed in the job for lack of anywhere else to go.

entries.ipa: /fɔr ˈwɑnt əv/, also /ˈwɔnt/, weak /fɚ ˈwɑnt ə/, stressed for /fɔr/
entries.register: neutral to literary — proverbial, and noticeably formal in American English
entries.complement: noun phrase, usually bare (for want of a nail). A gerund is possible but unusual. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] for want of [noun phrase] / For want of [noun phrase], [clause] / for want of a better [noun] / for want of anything better to do
entries.contrast: Identical in meaning to for lack of; the whole difference is register. Want appears here in its old sense of absence, shortage, which survives in modern American English almost nowhere else (wanting, in want of, for want of). Because that sense is opaque to most speakers, choosing for want of reads as a deliberate stylistic gesture rather than a neutral choice.
entries.meaning: The literary twin of for lack of: it names an absence as the cause of a failure, using want in its old sense of shortage.
examples: For want of a nail the shoe was lost.
The bill failed for want of a second.
He called it a memoir, for want of a better term.
A dozen small farms went under for want of rain.
She read the manual twice for want of anything better to do.
The motion was denied for want of jurisdiction.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈlaɪt əv/, weak /ɪn ˈlaɪt ə/, run together as /ɪn ˈlaɪtə/
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in light of having missed two payments). Never a finite clause — use in light of the fact that if you must have one.
entries.pattern: In light of [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] in light of [noun phrase] / in light of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: In light of names the information that leads someone to a decision, not the physical force that produces an event. You cancel a launch in light of the forecast, but the rocket does not explode in light of a faulty valve — that is because of. Against in view of, the two are near-identical; in light of is commoner in American English and suggests something newly learned, while in view of suggests a standing circumstance.
variants: in the light of (dominant British form; American English strongly prefers in light of)
entries.meaning: Names the new information or evidence in the light of which a decision is taken or reconsidered.
examples: In light of the new evidence, the district attorney reopened the case.
The board postponed the vote in light of the auditor's report.
In light of everything that's happened, a delay seems reasonable.
The policy was rewritten in light of last year's lawsuit.
In light of his record, the judge suspended the sentence.
We reconsidered in light of having lost two of our biggest accounts.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈvju əv/, weak /ɪn ˈvju ə/
entries.register: formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a finite clause — in view of the fact that for a clause.
entries.pattern: In view of [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] in view of [noun phrase] / in view of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: The literal spatial phrase in view of — within sight of, as in a cabin in view of the lake — is a different animal and is not a preposition of cause; only the abstract use belongs here, and context always separates them. Against in light of: both name grounds for a decision, but in view of points at a circumstance already in place (in view of his age) where in light of points at something newly learned (in light of the report). Both are more formal than given and much more formal than since.
entries.meaning: Names the standing circumstance that a decision takes account of — the formal way of saying given.
examples: In view of his age, the court imposed probation instead.
The fee was waived in view of the delay on our end.
In view of the weather, the ceremony has been moved indoors.
The trial was halted early in view of the risks involved.
No further action was taken in view of the company's cooperation.
In view of having already paid twice, she refused the third invoice.

entries.ipa: /ɑn əˈkaʊnt əv/, weak /ən əˈkaʊnt ə/, casual /ənəˈkaʊntə/
entries.register: neutral in writing, colloquial in speech — and the clause use is nonstandard
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (on account of being sick). In standard written English, never a finite clause — but on account of he was sick, with a full clause, is a real and widespread spoken form in Southern, Midland, and African American English, and the folk-doubled on account of because belongs to the same register. Recognize both; do not write either in edited prose.
entries.pattern: [clause] on account of [noun phrase] / On account of [noun phrase], [clause] / on account of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: A plain synonym of because of — one register down in speech, one register up in older writing. Do not confuse the causal preposition with the accounting phrase on account (as partial payment) or with on someone's account (for someone's sake): don't stay on my account means not for my sake, not not because of me.
entries.meaning: Names a cause in the plainest available words, with a spoken flavor that because of does not have.
examples: School was closed on account of the ice.
On account of the recall, we're two weeks behind.
He couldn't travel on account of his knee.
She got the extension on account of being in the hospital.
The store closed early on account of the power outage.
On account of the drought, the town banned outdoor watering.
related: on account of the fact that (conjunction)

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈɡraʊndz əv/, weak /ən ðə ˈɡraʊndz ə/
entries.register: formal and legal
entries.complement: noun phrase — characteristically an abstract noun naming a category of justification (race, cruelty, national security, self-incrimination). A gerund is possible but stiff. Never a finite clause: the clause form is on the grounds that, which is a conjunction, not this preposition.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the grounds of [noun phrase] / [clause] on grounds of [noun phrase] / on the grounds that [clause] (the conjunction)
entries.contrast: On the grounds of + noun phrase, on the grounds that + clause is the pair to memorize; splicing them (on the grounds of he lied) is the standard error. Against because of, this phrase names a justification somebody offered, not a cause operating in the world: a permit is denied on the grounds of zoning, but a roof does not collapse on the grounds of snow. Against on the basis of, which points at evidence rather than at a reason for a decision. Against on the pretext of, which is the same phrase with the writer's judgment added: on the grounds of leaves open whether the stated reason is the true one, on the pretext of says it is not.
variants: on grounds of (standard in journalism and legal drafting)
on the ground of (older, now mainly British)
entries.meaning: Names the stated justification for a decision, a refusal, a claim, or a legal action.
examples: The claim was denied on the grounds of a pre-existing condition.
Discrimination on the grounds of age is prohibited.
He refused to testify on the grounds of self-incrimination.
The documents were withheld on grounds of national security.
She filed on the grounds of desertion.
The appeal was rejected on the grounds of untimeliness.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈpritɛkst əv/, weak /ən ðə ˈpritɛkst ə/
entries.register: neutral to formal — journalism, history, and narrative
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (on the pretext of checking the meter). Never a finite clause — the clause form is on the pretext that + clause, which is a conjunction: on the pretext that the meter needed checking.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the pretext of [verb-ing] / [clause] under the pretext of [noun phrase] / on the pretext that [clause] (the conjunction)
entries.contrast: The dishonest twin of on the grounds of. Both name a stated reason rather than an operating cause, but on the grounds of is neutral about whether the stated reason is the real one, while on the pretext of asserts that it is not: a permit denied on the grounds of zoning may well be about zoning, but a search conducted on the pretext of a broken taillight is not about the taillight. Because the phrase commits the writer to that judgment, you cannot use it of your own motives except as a joke. Against in the name of, which names a value invoked as cover and leaves the sincerity open.
variants: under the pretext of (at least as common in American English; a shade more accusatory)
on the pretense of (near-synonym)
under the guise of (stresses the disguise rather than the excuse)
entries.meaning: Names the false reason somebody gave — the excuse offered to cover the real motive.
examples: He got into the building on the pretext of delivering a package.
The troops crossed the border under the pretext of a training exercise.
She left the table on the pretext of a call she had to take.
Editors killed the piece on the pretext of space, and everybody knew better.
Under the pretext of reviewing the budget, the committee reopened the whole contract.
He came by twice a week on the pretext of returning tools he had never borrowed.
The stop was made on the pretext of a broken taillight.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈstrɛŋkθ əv/, also /ˈstrɛŋθ/, weak /ən ðə ˈstrɛŋkθ ə/
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (on the strength of having worked with them before). Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the strength of [noun phrase] / On the strength of [noun phrase], [clause] / on the strength of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Names the evidence or asset somebody relied on when they acted — a recommendation, a demo, one good quarter. Because of would state the cause flatly; on the strength of says the actor weighed something and found it convincing, and it carries a faint hint that the weighing may yet prove to have been optimistic. Against by virtue of, which names a standing status rather than a demonstration, and against on the basis of, which is colder and more procedural.
entries.meaning: Names the demonstration, showing, or asset that persuaded someone to act.
examples: She was hired on the strength of one interview.
The bank lent them the money on the strength of a signed letter of intent.
On the strength of two good quarters, the board approved the expansion.
He got the part on the strength of a two-minute audition tape.
The town issued bonds on the strength of projected tourism revenue.
They took the deal on the strength of having worked with the buyer before.

entries.ipa: /ˈaʊt əv/, weak /ˈaʊtə/
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: in the motive sense (1), a bare abstract noun with no determiner — out of curiosity, out of spite, out of respect, out of habit. An article usually breaks it: out of a sense of duty works only because the head noun is sense, while out of the curiosity is impossible. A gerund is marginal in this sense (out of not wanting to embarrass her occurs and grates). In the source sense (2) the complement is an ordinary noun phrase with its determiners intact — out of that meeting, out of one complaint letter — and a fused relative works there as well, which is still a noun phrase and not a clause: something good came out of what happened. In the exhaustion sense (3) it is again a bare noun, this time naming a resource: out of options, out of time, out of patience. Never a that-clause in any sense, and no other finite clause either. Bare out is a different word: it is an adverb or a verb particle and takes no object at all (she walked out, cross it out, the truth came out), where out of is the two-word preposition and always requires one — the truth came out against the truth came out of a deposition nobody read. The spatial out of (out of the house) is treated with the prepositions of movement, and the full six-sense account of the word, proportions and made out of included, is at out of (complex prepositions).
entries.pattern: [clause] out of [bare abstract noun] / Out of [bare abstract noun], [clause] / out of a sense of [noun] / out of respect / fear / spite / habit / necessity / curiosity / desperation / [come / grow / arise / develop] out of [noun phrase] / Out of [resource noun], [clause]
entries.contrast: In sense 1 out of names the motive inside the actor — the feeling or disposition the action came out of — where because of names a cause outside. She lied out of fear is about her state; she lied because of the threat is about the threat. The determinerless noun is the surest sign you are in this sense rather than the spatial one. Against from, which overlaps in acted from a sense of duty but sounds more literary. Sense 2 is the ancestor of the legal arising out of, and there the direction reverses: the object is the origin and the subject is what grew from it. Sense 3 is the mirror of for lack of — both make an absence the reason — but for lack of names what was never there and out of names what ran out.
entries.meaning: 1. The motive inside the actor. The feeling, disposition, or state of mind an action springs from, named by a bare abstract noun. I asked out of curiosity. 2. The source something developed from. With verbs of emergence — come, grow, arise, develop — naming the episode a later thing grew out of. The whole program grew out of one complaint letter. 3. The resource run down to nothing, offered as a reason. Almost always fronted and absolute, naming the shortage that forced the outcome. Out of options, they settled.
examples: I asked out of curiosity, not because I doubted her.
He kept the letters out of sentiment.
They took the dog in out of pity.
She resigned out of loyalty to her staff, not out of anger.
Most of them show up out of habit.
He agreed out of sheer exhaustion.
The company recalled the batch out of an abundance of caution.
The whole program grew out of one complaint letter.
Nothing useful came out of the second meeting.
Two good ideas came out of an afternoon nobody had wanted to sit through.
Out of options and nearly out of time, they settled on the courthouse steps.
Out of patience with a third round of revisions, she pulled the piece.

entries.ipa: /ˈoʊvər/ (no weak form; the clipped o'er /ɔr/ is verse only)
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund (sued over failing to disclose the defect), or a wh-clause — and the wh-clause is the one complement that separates over from every other word in this file: a dispute over whether the vote was binding, confusion over how the money was spent, a fight over who pays. Never a that-clause: an argument over that he lied is not English. Over is also an adverb (the meeting is over, pull over, come over), an adjective (it's over between them), and a verb particle (think it over, hand it over); the preposition always has an object and the adverb never does — they argued over the fee against the argument is over, he handed over the keys against he leaned over the rail.
entries.pattern: [noun or verb of conflict, loss, or strong feeling] over [noun phrase] / resign / quit / sue / be arrested / cry / agonize / apologize / lose sleep over [noun phrase] / fuss / gush / fawn / rave / obsess over [noun phrase] / disagreement / confusion / a fight over [wh-clause] / stranded: what exactly are they fighting over?
entries.contrast: This entry covers only the sense the thing that provoked it. Over's spatial and path senses live with the prepositions of movement, its span sense with those of time, its quantity sense with those of measure, and its neutral topic use is worked out under topic and reference. Against about: about is neutral, over has friction — you talk about money and fight over it. Against because of: because of attaches to any verb at all, but over needs a verb or noun that already implies conflict, loss, or strong feeling, which is why he resigned over the memo works and he arrived over the memo does not.
entries.meaning: 1. The point of contention — what two parties are in conflict about. A ten-year fight over water rights. 2. The trigger of a strong reaction — a resignation, a lawsuit, an arrest, a firing. He resigned over the handling of the complaint. 3. The object of grief, worry, or regret — what somebody frets or mourns about. There's no use crying over spilled milk. 4. The object of a fuss — what somebody makes too much of, admiring as readily as complaining. They fussed over the baby all afternoon.
examples: The strike began as an argument over scheduling software.
Two counties have been in court over the same forty acres since 2003.
Congress deadlocked over the disaster funding bill.
There is still disagreement over whether the vote was binding.
Nobody could explain the confusion over how the money had been spent.
The deputy director resigned over the handling of the complaint.
The city was sued over the condition of the pumping station.
Two officers were suspended over failing to report the incident.
He's still beating himself up over one bad quarter.
She lost a week's sleep over a two-line email.
There's no use crying over spilled milk.
The whole family fussed over the baby for an hour.
Critics raved over a record the band itself had written off.

entries.ipa: /ˈoʊɪŋ tu/, weak /ˈoʊɪŋ tə/
entries.register: formal, and somewhat old-fashioned in American English
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (owing to being short-staffed). Never a finite clause — owing to the fact that for a clause. Keep it separate from the ordinary predicative adjective owing (there is still money owing), where no preposition is involved at all.
entries.pattern: [clause] owing to [noun phrase] / Owing to [noun phrase], [clause] / owing to [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Traditional usage guides recommended owing to in precisely the position where they forbade adverbial due to, so Owing to fog, the flight was canceled was the sanctioned version of Due to fog, the flight was canceled. That is essentially why the phrase still exists: it is the escape hatch from a rule most Americans no longer apply. In present-day American English it reads as bookish or British, and because of does the same work in the same number of syllables.
entries.meaning: Names a cause, in a register one notch above because of. Frozen out of the verb owe, it is the phrase the old due to rule left standing.
examples: Owing to a shortage of parts, deliveries have slipped by a month.
The concert was canceled owing to illness.
Attendance was down owing to the weather.
Owing to circumstances beyond our control, the office will be closed Friday.
The bridge was closed owing to structural concerns.
Owing to having lost their star witness, the prosecution offered a plea.

entries.ipa: /ˈθæŋks tu/, weak /ˈθæŋks tə/
entries.register: neutral — common in speech and in journalism
entries.complement: noun phrase, including an objective-case pronoun (thanks to you, thanks to them). A gerund is possible but uncommon. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] thanks to [noun phrase] / Thanks to [noun phrase], [clause] / no thanks to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The only causal preposition with an attitude built into it. Literally it credits a benefactor; in practice it is at least as often sarcastic, and the sarcasm rides entirely on whether the result is good or bad — thanks to her, we finished early against thanks to her, we missed the flight. The negative no thanks to reverses it once more and names someone who actively did not help. Because of is the neutral word when you want none of this.
entries.meaning: 1. Crediting the cause of something good. Thanks to a tailwind, we landed early. 2. Blaming the cause of something bad — ironic, and just as frequent. Thanks to the detour, we sat in traffic for an hour. 3. No thanks to: naming someone whose contribution was zero or negative. We made it, no thanks to you.
examples: Thanks to a tailwind, we landed twenty minutes early.
She got through school thanks to a scholarship and two jobs.
Thanks to the new software, closing the books takes a day instead of a week.
Thanks to the detour, we sat on the shoulder for an hour.
Thanks to whoever left the gate open, the dog is somewhere in the next county.
We made the deadline, no thanks to the vendor.
The town has a library thanks to one stubborn donor.
Thanks to a clerical error, she got two paychecks in March and had to give one back.
The whole neighborhood floods now, thanks to the parking lot they put in upstream.

entries.ipa: /θru/ — no true weak form, but in rapid speech the vowel shortens toward /θrʊ/ and, before a consonant, as far as /θrə/ (through carelessness /θrə ˈkɛrləsnəs/)
entries.register: neutral, a shade formal in this sense
entries.complement: in the causal sense, a noun phrase headed by an abstract noun naming a fault, quality, or process — through carelessness, through sheer luck, through neglect — very often with no determiner. A gerund is marginal. Never a finite clause. Through is also an adverb (let me through, the bolt went through), an adjective (we're through, are you through with that?), and a time preposition (Monday through Friday); the preposition always has an object and the adverb never does — it failed through carelessness (preposition plus object) against pull the wire through and he read it through (adverb, no object of its own). Note too that the movement sense strands freely (the tunnel we drove through) while this causal sense does not: What did the file get deleted through? is not idiomatic.
entries.pattern: [clause] through [abstract noun] / Through [abstract noun], [clause] / through no fault of [possessive] own / through sheer [noun]
entries.contrast: Through names the failing or the quality by which something came about, and it is at its most natural when blame is being assigned or denied — which is why the commonest instance of it in American English is the fixed exculpatory phrase through no fault of his own. Against because of, it is slightly more formal and far fussier about its object: through carelessness is idiomatic, through the rain is not. Against by, which names an agent or a method (by mistake, by the treasurer), where through names a quality that let the thing happen. Keep this entry apart from the means and intermediary sense — I heard it through a friend, file it through the regional office, sold through a broker — which takes an ordinary noun phrase naming a person, organization, or channel and is worked out under agent, instrument, and manner. The path, span, and completion senses live with movement and time.
entries.meaning: 1. The failing that let it happen — blame assigned or, just as often, denied. The file was deleted through carelessness. 2. The favorable quality, effort, or accident that let it happen. Through sheer luck, nobody was standing under it.
examples: The file was deleted through carelessness, not malice.
They lost the account through their own inattention.
He was laid off through no fault of his own.
The error crept in through a failure to check the second column.
The seat was lost through a clerical error nobody caught until Thursday.
Two of the three charges fell away through the state's own delay.
Through sheer luck, nobody was standing under it.
She learned the trade through years of watching her father.
Through stubbornness more than talent, he finished the degree in three years.

entries.ipa: /ˈwʌt wɪθ/, also /ˈwɑt/, older /ˈhwʌt/, weak /wət wəθ/, also /wət wəð/
entries.register: informal and conversational — rare in edited prose
entries.complement: a noun phrase, very often a coordinated list, and very often rounded off with and all. It also takes a small clause — a noun phrase plus a participle, as in what with the kids being sick — which no other causal preposition does. Never a finite clause: what with he was sick is not English.
entries.pattern: What with [noun phrase] and [noun phrase], [clause] / What with [noun phrase] and all, [clause] / What with [noun phrase] [verb-ing], [clause] / [clause], what with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: What with differs from because of in two ways that matter. It almost always introduces several contributing causes rather than one, and it is apologetic — it explains away a shortfall rather than reporting a cause. What with the move and the new baby, we never sent cards is an excuse; because of the move, we never sent cards is a report. The what is a frozen relic with no meaning of its own: you cannot question it, stress it, or replace it.
entries.meaning: Introduces a pile of contributing circumstances, usually by way of excuse for something that did not get done.
examples: What with the move and the new baby, we never got the cards out.
What with one thing and another, the whole afternoon was gone.
What with gas and tolls, driving isn't any cheaper.
What with the kids being sick all week, nothing got done.
What with the storm and all, hardly anybody showed up.
She's exhausted, what with two jobs and a night class.

entries.ipa: /əˈraɪzɪŋ frʌm/, weak /əˈraɪzɪŋ frəm/
entries.register: legal — contracts, insurance policies, pleadings
entries.complement: noun phrase. No gerund in practice, and never a finite clause. Unlike almost everything else in this file it cannot be fronted: it postmodifies a noun, so there is no Arising from the accident, he sued.
entries.pattern: [noun] arising from [noun phrase] / [noun] arising out of or relating to [noun phrase] / any claim arising out of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: A participial phrase that has hardened into a fixed causal preposition inside legal boilerplate, where its very breadth is the point — arising out of or relating to this Agreement is drafted to sweep in everything a court might otherwise exclude. Against resulting from, which is narrower and implies direct causation, and caused by, narrower still. Drafters stack all three because courts read them as different widths of the same idea.
variants: arising out of (the standard form in American contract drafting)
arising under (narrower: deriving from the terms of the instrument itself)
entries.meaning: Names the event or instrument that a claim, cost, obligation, or dispute grew out of. Its object is the cause, and the noun it modifies is the result.
examples: Any dispute arising from this contract shall be settled by arbitration.
The policy excludes losses arising from flood.
She filed a claim for injuries arising from the collision.
Costs arising from the delay will be borne by the contractor.
All obligations arising from the merger survive termination.
The report covers complaints arising out of the November outage.

entries.ipa: /æz ə ˈkɑnsəkwɛns əv/, weak /əz ə ˈkɑnsəkwəns ə/
entries.register: formal — academic and technical writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (as a consequence of having missed the deadline). Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] as a consequence of [noun phrase] / As a consequence of [noun phrase], [clause] / as a direct consequence of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The heavier twin of as a result of. Consequence carries a faint suggestion that the outcome was foreseeable or that it matters morally — as a consequence of the policy implies the policy had a logic that led here, where as a result of merely reports the sequence. Both are longer than because of and neither adds anything a careful because of could not carry. Remember the direction: what follows is the cause.
entries.meaning: Names the cause an outcome followed from, with a suggestion that the outcome was foreseeable or consequential. What follows the phrase is the cause, not the consequence.
examples: Sea ice has thinned as a consequence of two unusually warm winters.
As a consequence of the merger, three plants were closed.
Enrollment fell sharply as a consequence of the tuition increase.
Several species disappeared as a consequence of the dam.
As a consequence of having missed the filing deadline, the firm lost its appeal.
The rule was suspended as a direct consequence of the court's ruling.

entries.ipa: /æz ə rɪˈzʌlt əv/, weak /əz ə rɪˈzʌltə/
entries.register: neutral to formal — the standard phrase of reports, news writing, and official statements
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (as a result of being denied a permit). Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] as a result of [noun phrase] / As a result of [noun phrase], [clause] / as a direct result of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: What follows as a result of is the cause. The phrase is built out of the word result, and that misleads people constantly. Compare the adverb as a result, with no of, which points the opposite way and needs no object at all: The crash closed the highway; as a result, four people were late. Against because of, this is three syllables longer and slightly more formal, and it is the better choice when the causal chain is indirect or has several links.
entries.meaning: Names the cause that an outcome followed from. The object of the phrase is the cause; the main clause reports the result.
examples: Four people were hospitalized as a result of the crash.
As a result of the recall, production has been halted at two plants.
Property values rose as a result of the new rail line.
She lost her license as a result of the second conviction.
As a result of being denied a permit, the festival moved across the river.
Nothing changed as a direct result of the report.

entries.ipa: /ˈkɔzd baɪ/, weak /ˈkɔzd bə/
entries.register: neutral — the plainest causal participle in the language, at home everywhere from warranties to weather reports
entries.complement: noun phrase naming either an event or, unusually for this file, an agent: damage caused by the contractor as readily as damage caused by the storm. A gerund is possible but stiff (caused by having left the valve open). Never a finite clause — there is no caused by that and no caused by the fact that worth writing.
entries.pattern: [noun] caused by [noun phrase] / [noun] was caused by [noun phrase] / damage / delay / injury / illness caused by [noun phrase] / arising out of, resulting from, or caused by [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The narrowest of the result phrases, and the test the whole due to dispute is built around: where caused by fits, adjectival due to is safe under every analysis. Against resulting from, which names a process rather than an agent, and arising from, which claims only connection; drafters stack all three because courts read them as three widths of one idea. Against because of, the difference is grammatical rather than semantic: because of is adverbial and fronts freely, while caused by follows be or postmodifies a noun and does not front — Caused by fog, the flight was canceled is not English.
entries.meaning: Attaches a result-noun, or a subject after be, to the thing that directly produced it. Like everything in this section its object is the cause.
examples: Most of the damage was caused by water, not by the fire itself.
Delays caused by the strike are excluded from the schedule.
The outage was caused by a squirrel in a substation.
Illness caused by contaminated well water accounted for half the cases.
Any injury caused by misuse of the ladder voids the warranty.
The crack was caused by settling, and the engineer put that in writing.
Losses arising out of, resulting from, or caused by flood are not covered.

entries.ipa: /ˈkɑnsəkwɛnt ɑn/, weak /ˈkɑnsəkwənt ən/
entries.register: formal and academic; in American English it is rare and slightly stiff
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [noun] consequent on [noun phrase] / [clause], consequent on [noun phrase] / [noun] consequent upon [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Unlike everything else in this section, consequent on is built on an adjective, so it most naturally postmodifies a noun (the layoffs consequent on the merger) rather than modifying a clause. Do not confuse it with the adverb consequently, which introduces the result rather than the cause, or with the noun consequence. What follows is the cause.
variants: consequent upon (older and heavier; commoner in British writing)
consequent to (occurs, but disliked by careful writers)
entries.meaning: An adjective-based phrase that attaches a result-noun to its cause: the layoffs consequent on the merger. What follows is the cause.
examples: The layoffs consequent on the merger were announced in March.
Erosion consequent on the removal of the dune line has accelerated.
Changes consequent upon the new statute take effect in July.
The board addressed the liabilities consequent on the recall.
Delays consequent on the strike pushed the opening to fall.
The illness consequent upon prolonged exposure is well documented.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈkɑnsəkwəns əv/, weak /ɪn ˈkɑnsəkwəns ə/
entries.register: formal, legal, and dated — nineteenth-century in flavor
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in consequence of [noun phrase] / In consequence of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The most old-fashioned member of the consequence family and the least used in modern American English; as a result of has replaced it nearly everywhere outside deeds, wills, and older statutes. The bare adverb in consequence (consequently) is a separate item that takes no object. As everywhere in this section, the object is the cause.
entries.meaning: The dated, legal way of naming the cause an outcome followed from. Its object is the cause, not the consequence.
examples: In consequence of the fire, the lease was declared void.
The estate passed to his nephew in consequence of the earlier bequest.
In consequence of these findings, the license was revoked.
Several officers were dismissed in consequence of the inquiry.
In consequence of her refusal to appear, the matter was continued.
The town lost its charter in consequence of the annexation.

entries.ipa: /rɪˈzʌltɪŋ frʌm/, weak /rɪˈzʌltɪŋ frəm/
entries.register: neutral to formal — technical, legal, insurance, and medical writing
entries.complement: noun phrase. A gerund is possible but rare (resulting from having ignored the warning), and there is never a finite clause. Like arising from it cannot be fronted: it postmodifies a noun, so there is no Resulting from the crash, four people were hurt.
entries.pattern: [noun] resulting from [noun phrase] / any damage / loss / injury resulting from [noun phrase] / [noun] stemming from [noun phrase] / arising out of or resulting from [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Narrower than arising from: resulting from claims direct causation where arising from claims only connection, which is exactly why drafters use both instead of choosing between them. The object is the cause and the noun in front is the result — the same direction trap as as a result of. Against caused by, which is narrower again and will name an agent (damage caused by the contractor) as readily as an event.
variants: stemming from (the everyday journalistic equivalent)
flowing from (a drafting alternate)
caused by (plainer and narrower still)
entries.meaning: Attaches a result-noun to the event that directly produced it. It is a participle that has hardened into a preposition, and like every phrase in this section its object is the cause.
examples: Any damage resulting from misuse is not covered by the warranty.
Injuries resulting from the collapse were treated at the scene.
Savings resulting from the merger will be reinvested in the plant.
The company denied liability for delays resulting from the strike.
Charges stemming from the November raid were dropped last week.
Complications resulting from the second surgery kept her in the hospital another week.
Costs arising out of or resulting from a breach are borne by the breaching party.

entries.ipa: /ˈsɛkənˌdɛri tu/, weak /ˈsɛkənˌdɛri tə/
entries.register: technical — medicine, epidemiology, and engineering reports; outside them it reads as jargon
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically a condition, event, or process (secondary to diabetes, secondary to blunt trauma). A gerund is rare and clinical (secondary to having aspirated). Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [noun] secondary to [noun phrase] / [condition] is secondary to [condition] / renal failure secondary to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: In this sense secondary to means caused by, not less important than, and the two senses share a spelling: renal failure secondary to diabetes names a cause, while cost is secondary to safety ranks two things. Only the causal sense belongs here, and context always separates them. Against attributable to, which assigns a measured share of an effect; secondary to asserts a chain instead — a primary condition and the one that followed from it. Against caused by, which is the plain-English version and the one to use with any reader outside the field. Like attributable to it follows be or postmodifies a noun and does not front: Secondary to diabetes, she was admitted is not English.
entries.meaning: Names the primary condition or event that a later one developed out of — the clinical way of saying caused by.
examples: She was admitted with renal failure secondary to long-standing diabetes.
The bleeding was secondary to a tear in the lining, not to the medication.
Hearing loss secondary to repeated infections is common in this group.
Deaths secondary to the storm went on for two weeks after landfall.
The fracture was secondary to a fall, and the fall was secondary to low blood pressure.
Most of the corrosion is secondary to a drainage failure on the upstream side.

entries.ipa: /fɔr ˈfɪr əv/, weak /fɚ ˈfɪr ə/, also /fər/, stressed for /fɔr/
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (for fear of waking her). Never a finite clause — the clause form is for fear that + clause, which is a conjunction: for fear that she would wake.
entries.pattern: [clause] for fear of [verb-ing] / [clause] for fear of [noun phrase] / for fear that [clause] (the conjunction)
entries.contrast: Negative purpose. The action is taken to avoid what follows, not to bring it about, which reverses the direction of every other phrase in this section: he stayed home for the sake of his health aims at health, he stayed home for fear of infection aims away from infection. For fear of + gerund and for fear that + clause are freely interchangeable and mean the same thing; splicing them (for fear of she would wake) is the error to watch. Lest is the literary conjunction with the same meaning.
entries.meaning: Negative purpose: names the outcome the action is designed to avoid.
examples: She whispered for fear of waking the baby.
Nobody spoke up, for fear of losing their jobs.
He wouldn't sign it for fear of a lawsuit.
The witnesses stayed anonymous for fear of retaliation.
They kept the diagnosis quiet for fear of worrying their daughter.
I didn't ask, for fear of the answer.

entries.ipa: /fɔr ðə ˈbɛnəfɪt əv/, weak /fɚ ðə ˈbɛnəfɪt ə/, stressed for /fɔr/
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a person, group, or institution. A gerund is not idiomatic here. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] for the benefit of [noun phrase] / For the benefit of [noun phrase], [clause] / held in trust for the benefit of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Names the beneficiary — who the action is meant to help — rather than the goal it aims at, which is what for the purpose of does. Against for the sake of, which also names a beneficiary but is warmer and, crucially, works with abstractions: for the sake of clarity is idiomatic where for the benefit of clarity is not. In law it is the fixed phrase for a trust beneficiary, and there it is not optional.
entries.meaning: Names the person, group, or institution an action is meant to serve.
examples: The fund is held in trust for the benefit of his grandchildren.
For the benefit of those just joining us, here's where we left off.
The recital was staged for the benefit of the music program.
She repeated the question for the benefit of the people in the back.
The easement exists for the benefit of the adjoining parcel.
He explained it twice, mostly for the benefit of the new hires.

entries.ipa: /fɔr ðə ˈpɜrpəs əv/, weak /fɚ ðə ˈpɜrpəs ə/, stressed for /fɔr/
entries.register: formal, legal, and bureaucratic
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund only — never a bare infinitive. For the purpose of determining eligibility is correct; for the purpose of to determine eligibility and for the purpose of determine eligibility are both errors. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] for the purpose of [verb-ing] / [clause] for the purpose of [noun phrase] / For the purposes of [this section / this Agreement], [clause]
entries.contrast: The great redundancy of official prose: nine times in ten, for the purpose of examining reduces to to examine with nothing lost. Keep the phrase where the plural is doing real work — for the purposes of this chapter, vehicle means... — because there it limits a definition rather than stating an aim. Against in order to, which takes the very infinitive this phrase forbids: the two are identical in meaning and opposite in grammar. Against in furtherance of, which names the larger scheme an act advances rather than the aim of the act itself.
variants: for purposes of
for the purposes of (the normal drafting form when fixing the scope of a document)
entries.meaning: 1. The aim of an act. The samples were collected for the purpose of establishing a baseline. 2. The scope within which a definition or a rule applies — the drafting plural, and the use worth keeping. For the purposes of this section, "resident" means...
examples: The samples were collected for the purpose of establishing a baseline.
He entered the building for the purpose of committing a felony.
The account was opened for the purpose of paying contractors.
Cameras were installed for the purpose of deterring theft, not surveillance.
She kept a separate notebook for the purpose of tracking expenses.
For the purposes of this section, "resident" means a person domiciled in the state.
For purposes of the rebate, a duplex counts as one dwelling.
Nothing in this paragraph limits the term for the purposes of Article IV.

entries.ipa: /fɔr ðə ˈseɪk əv/, weak /fɚ ðə ˈseɪk ə/, stressed for /fɔr/
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (for the sake of getting it over with). Never a finite clause. It also has a possessive frame with no of at all — for her sake, for the children's sake, for heaven's sake, for old times' sake, for its own sake — and note the bare apostrophe in for goodness' sake and for old times' sake.
entries.pattern: [clause] for the sake of [noun phrase] / For the sake of [noun phrase], [clause] / for the sake of [verb-ing] / for [possessive] sake / for the sake of argument / for its own sake
entries.contrast: Two jobs in one phrase. With a person it means for their benefit and overlaps for the benefit of, though it is warmer and more personal. With an abstraction — clarity, argument, simplicity, appearances — it means in order to achieve or preserve, and there nothing else substitutes: for the sake of clarity is fixed where for the benefit of clarity is not English. For the sake of argument means granting it provisionally, and for its own sake means as an end in itself.
entries.meaning: 1. For someone's benefit. They stayed together for the sake of the kids. 2. In order to get or preserve something abstract. For the sake of clarity, let's number them. 3. Fixed phrases: for the sake of argument, for its own sake, for heaven's sake.
examples: They stayed together for the sake of the children.
Do it for the sake of your mother, if not for mine.
For the sake of clarity, let's number the options.
He argued the other side for the sake of argument.
She studies Latin for the sake of the language itself, not for any use it has.
For heaven's sake, close the door.
They cut the last chapter for the sake of getting the book out on time.
She kept the old spelling for old times' sake and for nothing else.
For the sake of appearances, both of them came to the ribbon-cutting.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ən ˈɛfərt tu/, weak /ɪn ən ˈɛfɚt tə/
entries.register: neutral — the workhorse purpose phrase of American news writing
entries.complement: a bare infinitive verb, and nothing else — like in order to and so as to, and unlike every of-phrase in this section. In an effort to cut costs, never in an effort to cutting costs and never in an effort of cutting costs. Never a finite clause. The noun effort is still live inside the phrase, which is why it accepts adjectives no true preposition would: in a last-ditch effort to, in a renewed effort to, in a coordinated effort to.
entries.pattern: [clause] in an effort to [verb] / In an effort to [verb], [clause] / in a [adjective] effort to [verb] / in an attempt to [verb]
entries.contrast: Belongs with in order to and so as to on the infinitive side of the purpose split, not with with a view to and with the aim of on the gerund side — in an effort to reducing costs is the error, and it is common precisely because so many neighboring phrases end in of. Against in order to, it adds exertion and a hint of doubt: in an effort to reports that somebody tried, and often implies the trying may not have worked. Reporters reach for it constantly because it states a motive without endorsing it.
variants: in an attempt to (identical in grammar, a shade more tentative)
in a bid to (the headline version; commoner in British journalism)
entries.meaning: States the purpose of an action with an infinitive, adding the sense that somebody exerted themselves and may not have succeeded. Like in order to it can never take a noun or a gerund.
examples: The city cut bus fares in an effort to boost ridership.
In an effort to keep the plant open, the union agreed to a wage freeze.
She took a second job in an effort to stay ahead of the medical bills.
The agency rewrote the form in an effort to reduce filing errors.
In a last-ditch effort to save the season, the club fired its coach.
Regulators tightened the rule in an attempt to close the loophole.
He apologized twice in an effort to put the whole thing behind them.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈfɜrðərəns əv/, weak /ɪn ˈfɜrðərəns ə/
entries.register: legal and institutional — indictments, bylaws, trust instruments, and mission statements
entries.complement: noun phrase — a scheme, plan, conspiracy, policy, purpose, or interest. A gerund occurs (in furtherance of settling the claim) but is unusual and reads as drafting slack. Never a bare infinitive (in furtherance of to settle) and never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in furtherance of [noun phrase] / In furtherance of [noun phrase], [clause] / an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy / in furtherance of its charitable purposes
entries.contrast: Names the larger aim an act advances, where in pursuance of names an order the act carries out and for the purpose of names the aim of the act itself. The difference does real work in criminal law: an overt act in furtherance of a conspiracy need not accomplish anything at all — it only has to move the scheme along, which is why mailing a letter can be one. Against in pursuit of, which keeps the metaphor of a chase alive and can carry disapproval; in furtherance of is flat and institutional and passes no judgment.
entries.meaning: Names the larger plan, purpose, or interest that an act is meant to advance.
examples: The indictment alleges three overt acts in furtherance of the conspiracy.
The trustees may sell property in furtherance of the foundation's purposes.
In furtherance of the settlement, both parties agreed to a stay.
The grant was made in furtherance of the county's housing plan.
Nothing in this section authorizes a payment in furtherance of a private interest.
She was fired over an email sent in furtherance of the very policy she was accused of ignoring.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈɔrdər tu/, weak /ɪn ˈɔrdər tə/
entries.register: neutral, a shade more formal than bare to
entries.complement: a bare infinitive verb, and nothing else. In order to leave — never in order to departure, never in order to leaving. It cannot take a noun phrase at all, which is what disqualifies it as a preposition in the strict sense; it is an infinitival subordinator occupying a preposition's slot. The negative is in order not to. For a finite clause the form is in order that + clause, usually with may, might, or can, and it is formal. The frame in order for [noun phrase] to [verb] supplies a different subject: in order for this to work.
entries.pattern: [clause] in order to [verb] / In order to [verb], [clause] / in order not to [verb] / in order for [noun phrase] to [verb]
entries.contrast: The purpose phrases split cleanly by what they take. In order to, so as to, and in an effort to take an infinitive; for the purpose of, with a view to, with an eye to, with the aim of, and in the hope of take a gerund or a noun. Crossing the lists is the most reliable purpose error there is. Against bare to, which means exactly the same thing: in order is deletable in nearly every sentence, and its real work is removing ambiguity where a plain to could be read as something else — He stopped in order to talk is unmistakable, He stopped to talk is not always.
entries.meaning: States the purpose of an action with an infinitive. Strictly it is an infinitival subordinator rather than a preposition, since it can never take a noun; it is listed here because it competes directly with the gerund-taking purpose phrases.
examples: In order to qualify, you have to have lived here a year.
She left early in order to beat the traffic.
He took a second job in order to pay off the loan.
In order not to embarrass anyone, we'll skip the names.
In order for the warranty to apply, you have to register the unit.
The fund was created in order to keep the theater open.

entries.ipa: /ɪn pərˈsuəns əv/, weak /ɪn pərˈsuəns ə/
entries.register: legal and official; rare anywhere else
entries.complement: noun phrase — typically a document, power, duty, or policy. Gerunds are possible but unusual. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in pursuance of [noun phrase] / In pursuance of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Means in carrying out — the action gives effect to something already agreed or ordered. It is easily confused with pursuant to, which means in accordance with and points at authority rather than execution: you act pursuant to a statute because it permits you, and in pursuance of a policy because you are carrying it out. Distinguish both from in pursuit of, which names a thing chased (in pursuit of a suspect, in pursuit of happiness). American drafting prefers pursuant to and keeps in pursuance of mostly for older instruments. Against in furtherance of, which advances a scheme rather than executing an order.
entries.meaning: Names the order, policy, power, or agreement that an action is carrying out.
examples: The warrant was issued in pursuance of the court's order.
In pursuance of this policy, all contracts are now reviewed centrally.
The trustees acted in pursuance of the powers conferred by Article VI.
Notices given in pursuance of this section must be in writing.
In pursuance of the treaty, both governments reduced their tariffs.
He sold the property in pursuance of the settlement agreement.

entries.ipa: /ɪn pərˈsut əv/, weak /ɪn pɚˈsut ə/ (British /pəˈsjuːt/)
entries.register: neutral to formal, and a shade elevated
entries.complement: noun phrase — a goal, a quarry, or an abstraction (happiness, profit, a settlement, a suspect). A gerund is unusual and usually awkward: in pursuit of expanding the business is clumsy where with a view to expanding the business is not. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in pursuit of [noun phrase] / In pursuit of [noun phrase], [clause] / in hot pursuit of [noun phrase] / in dogged / relentless / single-minded pursuit of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Names the thing chased, where in pursuance of names the order being carried out. The two look almost identical and are unrelated: you act in pursuance of the court's order because you are executing it, and you drive in pursuit of a stolen pickup because you are chasing it. Against with the aim of, which takes a gerund and states a target coolly; in pursuit of keeps the metaphor of the chase alive, which lets it carry disapproval — in pursuit of profit at any cost judges, with the aim of increasing profit does not.
entries.meaning: Names the goal or the quarry an action is chasing, keeping the metaphor of the chase alive.
examples: He left a tenured job in pursuit of a startup idea.
Two cruisers went by in pursuit of a stolen pickup.
In pursuit of a Nobel, the lab spent a decade on a single protein.
The company cut corners in pursuit of a quarterly number.
Whole families moved west in pursuit of cheap land.
She reads three papers a day in pursuit of an edge nobody else has.
The deputies were in hot pursuit of a car that had run the checkpoint.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈhoʊp əv/, weak /ɪn ðə ˈhoʊp ə/
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a gerund or a noun phrase — never a bare infinitive. In the hope of finding work is correct; in the hope of to find work and in the hope to find work are both errors. Never a finite clause — the clause form is in the hope that + clause, which is a conjunction: in the hope that she would call.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the hope of [verb-ing] / [clause] in the hopes of [verb-ing] / In the hope of [verb-ing], [clause] / [clause] in the hope of [noun phrase] / in the hope that [clause] (the conjunction)
entries.contrast: The purpose phrase that concedes the purpose may not be reached. With the aim of states a target and expects to hit it; in the hope of states one and admits the odds. It sits on the gerund side of the purpose split with with a view to, with the aim of, and for the purpose of, and it attracts the identical infinitive error. Against for fear of, its exact mirror: one aims at a wanted outcome, the other away from an unwanted one — she wrote in the hope of an answer against she didn't write for fear of an answer.
variants: in the hopes of (common and fully standard in American English)
in hopes of (thoroughly American; no article)
entries.meaning: States a purpose while conceding it may not be reached. Its of is a preposition, so a verb after it must be a gerund.
examples: They moved to Phoenix in the hope of finding steady work.
He left the porch light on in the hopes of seeing her car pull in.
In the hope of settling before trial, both sides agreed to mediation.
She sent the manuscript out again in the hope of one honest reader.
The town rebuilt the pier in hopes of drawing summer traffic back.
He kept every receipt in the hope of a refund that never came.
In the hopes of heading off a strike, management reopened the contract.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ði ˈɪntrəst əv/, also /ˈɪntərəst/, weak /ɪn ðə ˈɪntrəst ə/
entries.register: neutral to formal — the institutional word
entries.complement: noun phrase — most often an abstract noun naming a value (time, fairness, safety, transparency, full disclosure) — or a party whose interests are being served, or a gerund, which is fully idiomatic here: in the interest of avoiding delay, in the interest of getting this done today. Never a bare infinitive (in the interest of to avoid delay) and never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: In the interest of [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] in the interest of [noun phrase] / in the interests of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Overlaps for the sake of in the abstract sense — in the interest of clarity and for the sake of clarity are interchangeable — and differs only in tone: in the interest of belongs to meetings, memos, and disclosures, where for the sake of is personal. With a party rather than a value it means to that party's advantage and shades toward for the benefit of.
variants: in the interests of (fully standard; the dominant British form. American English uses both, with the singular slightly ahead in edited prose)
entries.meaning: 1. The value an action is meant to serve. In the interest of time, let's take this offline. 2. The party an action is meant to advantage — nearly always the plural interests. The court sealed the file in the interests of the minor children.
examples: In the interest of time, let's take the rest of this offline.
The records were released in the interest of transparency.
In the interest of full disclosure, I own stock in the company.
In the interest of safety, the trail is closed until spring.
He recused himself in the interest of avoiding any appearance of bias.
The court sealed the file in the interests of the minor children.
The guardian may settle the claim in the interests of the estate.
Regulators blocked the deal in the interests of consumers, or said they had.

entries.ipa: /ˈsoʊ æz tu/, weak /soʊ əz tə/
entries.register: formal — commoner in writing than in speech
entries.complement: a bare infinitive verb, and nothing else — like in order to and unlike everything else in this section. So as to avoid delay, never so as to avoidance, never so as to avoiding. The negative so as not to is extremely common and is in fact the phrase's most frequent use. The understood subject of the infinitive must match the subject of the main clause; if it does not, the sentence dangles — So as to save time, the meeting was shortened leaves nobody saving time.
entries.pattern: [clause] so as to [verb] / [clause] so as not to [verb]
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with in order to in meaning, with two differences that matter. First, so as to is more formal and much rarer in speech. Second, it resists fronting: In order to save time, we skipped lunch is natural, So as to save time, we skipped lunch is stilted. It is at its most idiomatic in the negative, where so as not to wake her beats in order not to wake her every time. Keep it separate from the result correlative so ... as to (so cold as to be dangerous), which is a different construction with a word wedged in the middle.
entries.meaning: States purpose with an infinitive, in a register a step above in order to, and is at its most idiomatic in the negative so as not to. Like in order to it can never take a noun.
examples: He spoke quietly so as not to wake the baby.
Fold the corner so as to leave a half-inch margin.
They staggered the shifts so as to keep the line running.
She phrased it carefully so as not to commit to anything.
The panels are angled so as to catch the afternoon sun.
Pack the mugs in newspaper so as not to chip them.

entries.ipa: /wɪð ə ˈvju tu/, weak /wəð ə ˈvju tə/
entries.register: formal — business, diplomatic, and legal writing
entries.complement: a gerund or a noun phrase — never a bare infinitive. With a view to reducing costs is correct; with a view to reduce costs is an error, and a very common one, because the to looks like an infinitive marker and is not. It is a preposition, and prepositions take -ing. The test is substitution: if with a view to reduction works, the slot belongs to a preposition and the verb must be -ing. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] with a view to [verb-ing] / [clause] with a view to [noun phrase] / With a view to [verb-ing], [clause]
entries.contrast: The classic to-plus-gerund trap, in the same family as look forward to, be committed to, object to, and be used to. Against in order to, which takes the infinitive this phrase forbids — identical meaning, opposite grammar. Against with an eye to and with the aim of, which take the same gerund and sound less formal. With a view of is a different phrase entirely and means with a sight of: a room with a view of the harbor. Note that this is the one purpose phrase the of-test does not sort: it ends in to and still takes a gerund, which is why it has to be learned as an exception — compare with intent to defraud, where the to really is an infinitive marker.
entries.meaning: States a purpose or eventual intention behind an action, in formal register. Its to is a preposition, so the verb after it must be a gerund.
examples: The two sides met with a view to resolving the dispute before trial.
The land was bought with a view to eventual development.
Records are retained with a view to possible litigation.
She took the assistant's job with a view to learning the business.
With a view to cutting overhead, the firm subleased two floors.
The treaty was drafted with a view to the accession of new members.

entries.ipa: /wɪð ən ˈaɪ tu/, weak /wəð ən ˈaɪ tə/
entries.register: neutral — plainer than with a view to, and common in journalism
entries.complement: a gerund or a noun phrase — never a bare infinitive, exactly as with with a view to. With an eye to expanding, not with an eye to expand. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] with an eye to [verb-ing] / [clause] with an eye toward [noun phrase] / With an eye to [verb-ing], [clause]
entries.contrast: The everyday American equivalent of with a view to, and the one to reach for if you want the idea without the boardroom register. It adds a note of watchfulness — the purpose is being held in mind while something else is done — which is why it takes so naturally to toward. Keep it apart from with an eye on, which means monitoring rather than aiming: with an eye on the clock watches the clock, while with an eye to the clock would make the clock the goal.
variants: with an eye toward (American English prefers toward)
with an eye towards (chiefly British)
entries.meaning: States a purpose held in mind while something else is being done — the plain American equivalent of with a view to.
examples: They renovated the top floor with an eye to renting it out.
The city rezoned the district with an eye toward attracting light manufacturing.
She's taking statistics with an eye to graduate school.
The contract was written with an eye to the next negotiation.
With an eye toward the fall election, the governor delayed the announcement.
He buys used equipment with an eye to reselling it in the spring.

entries.ipa: /wɪð ɪnˈtɛnt tu/, weak /wəθ ɪnˈtɛnt tə/, also /wəð/
entries.register: legal — the standard mens rea formula of American criminal statutes and charging documents
entries.complement: a bare infinitive verb. With intent to defraud, with intent to distribute, with intent to deprive — never with intent to defrauding and never with intent of defrauding. It is the only with-purpose phrase on the infinitive side of the split, and it is there because there is no of in it. Never a finite clause — the clause form is with the intent that + clause.
entries.pattern: [verb] with intent to [verb] / with the intent to [verb] / possession with intent to distribute / with the intent that [clause] (the conjunction)
entries.contrast: The most useful minimal pair in this section: with intent to defraud (infinitive, no of) against with the intention of defrauding (gerund, with of). Same meaning, opposite grammar, and the of is the tell. The rule holds across the whole section — of takes the gerund, bare to takes the infinitive — with with a view to as the lone exception, since its to is a preposition. Against with the aim of, which is the everyday phrase: with intent to belongs where the purpose is an element somebody has to prove.
variants: with the intent to (the fuller statutory form; same infinitive)
with the intention of (NOT a variant: it takes a gerund, not an infinitive)
entries.meaning: States a purpose as an element of an offense or a legal act, in the infinitive frame American criminal statutes use.
examples: He was charged with possession with intent to distribute.
The statute reaches any false statement made with intent to deceive a federal agency.
Breaking and entering with intent to commit a felony carries the longer sentence.
She signed the transfer with intent to put the assets beyond her creditors' reach.
The complaint alleges he altered the log with the intent to mislead the auditors.
The forms were backdated with intent to claim a credit the company had already lost.
Loitering with intent to solicit was struck down as unconstitutionally vague.

entries.ipa: /wɪð ði ˈeɪm əv/, weak /wəð ði ˈeɪm ə/
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: a gerund or a noun phrase — never a bare infinitive. With the aim of reducing waste, not with the aim of to reduce waste and not with the aim to reduce waste (with the aim to does occur and is widely judged an error). Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] with the aim of [verb-ing] / [clause] with the aim of [noun phrase] / With the aim of [verb-ing], [clause]
entries.contrast: The plainest of the with-purpose phrases: with a view to is more formal, with an eye to more watchful, and with the aim of simply states the target. Where with the intention of replaces it, the emphasis shifts from the target to the actor's state of mind, which is exactly why criminal pleadings prefer intent. Note that they prefer it in the infinitive frame with intent to, not in this one: with intent to defraud against with the intention of defrauding, and never with the intention to defraud.
variants: with the intention of (stresses deliberateness; the legal preference)
with the goal of
with the object of
entries.meaning: States the goal an action is designed to reach, in plain neutral register, with a gerund after of.
examples: The program was set up with the aim of cutting emergency-room visits.
He wrote the memo with the aim of getting the decision on the record.
With the aim of speeding up review, the agency added two examiners.
They merged the two departments with the aim of eliminating duplicate work.
The study was designed with the aim of settling the question for good.
She entered the country with the intention of staying permanently.
